name: quantity
intent: Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident.
problem: Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.
context: Value-scope code in domain, engineering or integration layers that handles physical quantities - length, mass, time, temperature, energy, data volume, concentration. It pays off when values arrive with heterogeneous units (sensors, imports, user input, third parties), when derived quantities such as speed or density are computed, when users select a unit system for display, and when values must survive persistence and transport. The language decides how much of the guarantee is compile-time (units as type parameters, phantom/branded types) and how much is a runtime value object backed by a conversion table or unit registry.
benefits: Unit errors become inexpressible or loud at the first operation: six feet plus 180 pounds is a compile error, a DimensionalityError or an explicit failure instead of a silent 186.
One owner for conversion factors, rounding and the amount-plus-unit string grammar, so the rules stop drifting between features, services, reports and exports.
Unit-compatible arithmetic and comparison behave like numbers: 500 m + 3 km resolves through one documented conversion, and quantities remain orderable and equal in the sense the model defines.
Value semantics - immutable, cheap to pass, safe to cache and share - make it a natural value object inside an entity or aggregate instead of a pair of loose attributes that can drift apart.
Interfaces document themselves (weight: Mass, timeout: Duration) and persistence/API schemas get an explicit unit field that authors cannot forget to write down.
Enables dimensional algebra for derived quantities where units live in the type system (speed = length/time, force = mass x acceleration), instead of pre-declaring every combination as a number.
The currency-specific case (Money) is the same skeleton with volatile ratios and explicit rounding, so one concept covers physical quantities and money.
tradeoffs: Every measurement becomes a value object: an allocation or boxing step in dynamic languages and a wrapper in value-typed ones, which is measurable overhead in tight loops over large numeric arrays.

Granularity is a permanent commitment - one type per unit or quantity explodes the type space and the conversion matrix, while a single runtime-unit class loses compile-time checking and turns unit mistakes back into runtime failures.

Conversion factors become maintained data: a ratio table or unit registry that must be initialised and versioned, with floating-point factors that are inexact for most imperial conversions, so precision and rounding become part of the contract.

Affine units break ordinary arithmetic - absolute temperatures cannot meaningfully be added or multiplied - so the model must split absolute points from differentials or accept counter-intuitive algebra-preserving rules.
Equality, hashing and ordering must be decided together: if 1 km equals 1000 m then hash codes must agree, otherwise the value silently corrupts maps and sets; if it does not, users are surprised.
Persistence and transport need an explicit unit, and a column of mixed units makes SUM or AVG meaningless; JSON and FFI boundaries erase the unit unless a parser re-establishes it on arrival.
Printing and parsing add a grammar and a localisation surface (symbols versus names, prefixes, unit position) that has to be owned centrally or it diverges between clients and reports.

The simplest version forbids non-scalar multiplication and therefore gives up dimensional algebra, so derived units must be pre-declared; the sophisticated version costs metaprogramming complexity and compile time in C++, Rust and Scala.

participants.responsibility: The value itself: an amount paired with a unit, exposing unit-compatible addition and subtraction, comparison, conversion to another compatible unit, and amount-plus-unit printing/parsing; immutable, so every operation returns a new quantity.
The numeric part, expressed in the quantity's own unit - not a unit-free number, which is why it is only readable through the quantity (or through an explicit conversion accessor).

The scale and identity of the measurement: an atomic unit with its symbol, or a compound unit expressed as a product of powers (m/s, kg m/s^2); it knows how it relates to the dimension's base unit and, when formatting varies, how it prints.

The knowledge of how to convert between two units of one dimension - a scale factor, plus an offset for affine units such as temperatures; Fowler keeps it as a separate object, while libraries embed it in the unit or a converter.

The catalogue of known units and dimensions with their symbols, prefixes and base unit, providing lookup for parsing and the compatibility check that decides whether two quantities may be combined at all.
The boundary role: turns an amount plus a unit (or a written form such as '3 km') into a validated quantity and renders one back, so that validation and formatting do not spread across call sites.

use_cases: Sensor and telemetry pipelines where readings arrive tagged with a unit and must be normalised to a canonical unit before aggregation, alerting or storage.
Engineering and simulation code (CAD, robotics, structural, electrical) that computes derived quantities such as velocity, torque or energy and must keep the dimensions consistent.
Logistics and commerce where weight, dimensions and rate limits are expressed in different unit systems (kg/lb, cm/in, m^3/ft^3) and are displayed in the customer's chosen system.
Healthcare and laboratory systems that exchange doses and results between systems (mg/kg, mmol/L) with reference ranges in different units.
Energy and utility metering, where consumption (kWh, m^3) is billed through unit-price arithmetic and readings must be comparable across meter types.
UI-level unit-system switching: store and compute in one canonical unit, render and edit in metric or imperial according to a user preference.
Scientific Python applications built on Pint's UnitRegistry, such as sensor and laboratory pipelines, where quantities are parsed, converted and reduced dimensionally at integration boundaries.

.NET engineering and telemetry services using UnitsNet's strongly typed Length, Mass and related quantities, with parsing, conversion, serialization and display-unit selection centralized in the library.

Compile-time dimensional-analysis code using F# units of measure or C++ Boost.Units for simulation and control loops, where invalid unit arithmetic is rejected before runtime and derived units are expressed algebraically.
avoid_when: The system uses exactly one unit for a value everywhere, with no conversion and no display variation - a documented bare number, or a Newtype for the unit, is simpler and cheaper.
The unit is a presentation concern only: the domain always stores one canonical physical unit, so convert at the boundary and keep numbers inside.
The language or a library already gives compile-time units of measure (F# units of measure, uom, Boost.Units) - use those instead of a runtime quantity class.
The values are dimensionless counts, scores, indices or ratios that cannot meaningfully be converted into another unit.

Performance-critical inner loops over very large arrays of numbers: per-element quantity objects allocate and block vectorisation - use a raw array plus a documented scale, or a type-level unit that erases at runtime.
anti_patterns: The unit as free text: a struct with a String unit where conversion switches on string comparison, so a typo becomes a runtime error and no catalog can be trusted.

The god unit class: one Quantity with asMeters()/asFeet()/asInches()/asKilometres() members for every unit pair, collapsing under the combinatorial explosion instead of delegating to conversion ratios.
Affine units in arithmetic: adding two Celsius readings or multiplying Fahrenheit quantities, producing values that are physically meaningless but numerically plausible.
Unit information smuggled into names and comments - weightKg, distanceInFeet, a column comment - which is documentation that drifts the moment code is copied.
Converting to a bare float at every internal boundary and back, which erases the guarantee exactly where it was supposed to hold and reintroduces silent unit mix-ups.
design_principles: Whole value: an amount and its unit are one conceptual whole and belong in one type, not in two parallel attributes.
Single responsibility: conversion, rounding and formatting rules are owned by the quantity, the converter or the registry - never by call sites.
Fail fast: incompatible operations must be errors (compile-time where possible, explicit exceptions otherwise), never silently coerced numbers.
Immutability and value semantics: a quantity is a value - operations return new quantities, so it can be shared, cached and used as a map key safely.
Information hiding: the raw amount is not the interface; callers should go through the unit-aware operations so the unit cannot be dropped by accident.
Open/closed: new units arrive as data or new types in the catalogue, not as edits to arithmetic code.
best_practices: Persist and transmit the unit explicitly with every quantity, or make the per-context invariant explicit and enforced; never infer the unit from position, naming or column order.
Normalise to one canonical unit at the boundary (parse, ingest, load) and convert to display units only at the edge that renders or exports.
Keep conversion factors in one table or registry with documented precision, using scaled integers or exact rationals where round-trips must be lossless.
Make equality, hashing and ordering conversion-aware and consistent, or document unit-sensitive equality explicitly and expose a separate comparison in base units.
Model absolute affine quantities (temperature, pressure gauges) separately from their differentials, and forbid addition of absolutes while allowing differences.
Expose parsing and formatting for the amount-plus-unit form in one place with a documented grammar (SI symbols or UCUM), including prefixes and localisation decisions.
Decide explicitly whether multiplication and division of two quantities is allowed; if yes, provide the derived unit (compound unit algebra), if not, restrict to scalar scaling and document it.
Prefer a standard library or dominant framework package over hand-writing the quantity, conversion table and unit catalogue, and wrap it rather than forking it when conventions differ.
sources: Martin Fowler, Analysis Patterns: Reusable Object Models (1997), Chapter 3 'Observations and Measurements' - Quantity (pp. 36-38), Conversion Ratio (pp. 38-39), Compound Units (pp. 39-41).
Martin Fowler, Application Facades (1995), 'Implementing Quantity', p. 4 - the local amount-plus-unit pattern that the catalog row cites.
